content: The document outlines various radionuclides and their associated guidance levels, which were determined by averaging logarithmic scale values. These levels were rounded to the nearest order of magnitude, depending on whether the calculated value was below or above a specific threshold. The guidance levels are critical for ensuring radiological safety in drinking water and other applications. The annexes provide extensive references for further information on radionuclides, including publications by the International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP) and standards from the International Organization for Standardization (ISO). These references cover topics such as individual monitoring of radionuclide intake by workers, human alimentary tract models for radiological protection, and nuclear decay data for dosimetric calculations. Additionally, the document includes references to analytical methods and treatment technologies for radionuclides. These include techniques for removing natural radionuclides from drinking water, as well as methods for measuring radionuclide activity concentrations using high-resolution gamma-ray spectrometry, liquid scintillation counting, and alpha spectrometry. Specific standards, such as ISO 5667 for water sampling and ISO 9696 for measuring gross alpha and beta activity in water, are highlighted. The contributors to the development of these guidelines are acknowledged in the annex. These individuals and organizations have provided expertise through participation in meetings, authorship, peer review, and intellectual advice. The guidelines were developed with input from international experts, including representatives from the World Health Organization (WHO), national health agencies, universities, and environmental protection organizations. The document also lists specific contributors to the fourth edition of the Guidelines for Drinking-Water Quality, incorporating the first and second addenda. These contributors include professionals from various countries and institutions, such as the WHO, national public health agencies, universities, and independent consultants. Their work has been instrumental in shaping the guidelines and ensuring their scientific rigor. In summary, the document serves as a comprehensive resource for understanding radionuclide safety, water quality standards, and the methodologies used to monitor and manage radiological risks in water and the environment. It emphasizes the importance of international collaboration and adherence to standardized practices to protect public health.
